title: An ordinary morning (section 1)
hook: the Buddha dresses, walks for alms, eats, washes his feet and sits down

segments.voice: Yesterday, the turn, closed: three weeks of the Mahayana, from the bodhisattva to the book honored, a road wide enough for everyone. Your line: the great vehicle. Who did you make room for? Day one thousand one hundred eighteen.

A man gets up. He gets dressed. He picks up a bowl and walks into town to ask for food. He eats what he's given. He walks back. He puts the bowl away, washes his feet, and sits down. That's it. That's the whole first section of a great text of the Mahayana. No earthquake, no light from the sky, no gods arriving. Just a morning. For the next stretch of days, this path reads the Diamond Sutra, one short section a day. And it begins, on purpose or not, with chores.
screen: `DRESSED. BOWL. ALMS.` → `EAT. RETURN. WASH. SIT.` → `NO MIRACLE AT ALL.`

segments.voice: First, the name. In Sanskrit the sutra is the Vajracchedika. Max Müller's English translation titled it the Diamond-Cutter. People today call it the Diamond Sutra. Hold on to that name: a diamond, something hard enough to cut through other hard things. The sutra is going to cut. But not yet. Second, the scene, as the sutra sets it. It opens the old way: thus it was heard. The Buddha is staying near the city of Shravasti, in the Jeta grove, in the garden that Anathapindika gave, with a large company of monks. In the forenoon he puts on his robe, takes his bowl and cloak, and goes into the city for alms. He eats. He comes back from his round. He puts away his bowl and his cloak. He washes his feet. He sits on the seat prepared for him, legs crossed, body upright, his attention set before him. Then the monks come and sit nearby. Third, what the sutra doesn't say. It doesn't say the Buddha was thinking deep thoughts on the walk. It doesn't say the food was special or the feet were holy. Each act is simply done, then the next. The text moves at the speed of a person doing chores. Fourth, why start here. Some readers say this first section is already the whole teaching: before a word of wisdom is spoken, the Buddha shows it, by doing an ordinary morning completely and then sitting down. Others read it as the setting, the way any discourse opens. Either way, a text named for cutting begins with a bowl, a walk, and clean feet.
screen: `THE DIAMOND-CUTTER.` · `BOWL, ALMS, FEET, SEAT.` · `NOTHING SPECIAL IS SAID.` · `SHOWN BEFORE IT'S TAUGHT.` · then, large: `AN ORDINARY MORNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: do one morning chore fully. If you can, do it now. Wash a cup. Fold one shirt. Wipe a counter. Do it the way the sutra tells it: one act, then the next, nothing added. Feel the water's temperature. Notice the weight of the cup. When you're done, put the thing away, and sit down, the way he did, body upright, attention in front of you. If you can't get up, do it in memory: this morning's first chore, step by step, slowly. The bell holds the time.
Vajracchedika. The Diamond Sutra, the Diamond-Cutter in Max Müller's English, which opens on a plain morning of alms, a meal and washed feet. Today's word.

Your line: an ordinary morning. Tomorrow morning, do the first three things you do without your phone, each one finished before the next. Tomorrow, Subhuti asks. Day one thousand one hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: The Diamond Sutra is chanted and studied in Mahayana communities, Zen among them; it opens with the Buddha's alms round, meal and quiet sitting.

original.note: Sanskrit: the Diamond Sutra's name; Max Müller titled it the Diamond-Cutter.

trapdoor: what you thought: a great sutra would open with something dramatic.
what it means: the Diamond Sutra opens with the Buddha's ordinary morning, done fully, before a word is taught.
what a scholar hears: Max Müller's English calls it the Diamond-Cutter; the opening follows the frame of the older discourses, 'thus it was heard', at Shravasti in the Jeta grove.

notes: Section 1 is paraphrased from Max Müller's Vagrakkhedika (SBE 49, 1894) rather than quoted, since the exact wording wasn't verified. Check the order of acts (robe, bowl and cloak, alms, eating, return, put away, wash feet, sit cross-legged, upright, mindfulness before him; then the monks approach).
The text gives a number of monks (1,250 in Müller); the script says 'a large company' to avoid an unverified count.
'Diamond-Cutter' is given as Müller's title, not as an etymology.
howItsDone says the sutra is chanted and studied in Mahayana communities including Zen; confirm.
Devanagari spelling and stress guide for Vajracchedika should be checked.
